intro: These techniques build directly on Sorting & Binary Search: ternary search is binary search's cousin for unimodal (rather than monotonic) functions, custom comparators generalize 'sort then scan' by engineering the right sort key for a greedy or heap-based argument, and order statistics/quickselect reuse the partition step of quicksort to answer 'what is the k-th element' without fully sorting.

subtopics.name: Ternary Search on Unimodal Functions
subtopics.theory:
Binary search finds a target in a MONOTONIC function (or array); ternary search is the analogous tool for a UNIMODAL function -- one that strictly increases and then strictly decreases (or vice versa), with a single peak or valley. Given such a function f, pick two interior points m1 < m2 within the current search range [lo, hi] (commonly at the 1/3 and 2/3 marks). If f(m1) < f(m2) (searching for a maximum), the peak cannot lie to the left of m1, because f is still increasing there, so the range can be narrowed to [m1, hi]; symmetrically if f(m1) > f(m2), the peak cannot lie to the right of m2, so the range narrows to [lo, m2]. Each iteration discards roughly one-third of the range, giving O(log(range) / log(3/2)) iterations to converge -- still O(log n) asymptotically, just with a larger constant than binary search.

On a continuous (real-valued) domain, this is implemented with a fixed number of iterations (e.g. 100-200), since 'the range is small enough' has no natural integer stopping point; each iteration roughly multiplies the search interval width by 2/3, so 100 iterations shrink an initial range of 10^6 down to well below any double-precision-meaningful width. On an integer domain, care is needed: naive ternary search can infinite-loop or give an off-by-one wrong answer when the range becomes very small (comparing m1 and m2 might not make progress) or when the function has a PLATEAU (multiple adjacent points sharing the same optimal value) rather than a single strict peak. The standard robust fix is to shrink the search range only down to a small constant width (commonly hi - lo <= 2), using a comparison like 'if f(m1) <= f(m2) then hi = m2 else lo = m1 + 1', and then brute-force check the few remaining candidates directly -- this handles plateaus correctly because convexity still guarantees the true optimum survives every narrowing step, and the final brute-force sweep resolves any remaining ties exactly.

Recognizing unimodality is often the hard part, not implementing the search. Sums of convex functions are convex (and hence unimodal after negation for maximization), so if a cost function is built by summing several convex pieces (e.g. absolute-value costs, or a Kadane-style 'worst subarray sum' as a function of a shift parameter), the whole thing is guaranteed unimodal even without an explicit closed form -- letting you search on it directly without ever deriving a formula for the optimum.
subtopics.recognition: You need to optimize (minimize or maximize) a real- or integer-valued function of a single parameter, and you can argue (or it is given/provable) that the function first strictly increases then strictly decreases (or the reverse) -- i.e. it is unimodal/convex -- but you cannot easily solve for the optimum in closed form and each function evaluation is itself computable (e.g. via a linear scan or Kadane's algorithm).
subtopics.complexity: O(log(range)) evaluations of f for the search itself (each evaluation costing whatever it costs, e.g. O(n) for a Kadane-based check), so O(n log(range)) total for a typical 'search over a parameter, evaluate with a linear scan' problem.

examples.title: Minimizing the Weakness of a Sequence (real-valued ternary search)
examples.problem:
You are given n real numbers a[1..n]. For a chosen real number x, define the 'poorness' of a segment [l, r] as the absolute value of the sum (a[l]-x) + ... + (a[r]-x), and the 'weakness' of x as the maximum poorness over all non-empty contiguous segments. Find the value of x that minimizes the weakness, and print that minimum weakness.

Input: n, then n numbers a[1..n] (given as integers or decimals).
Output: the minimum possible weakness, printed with 6 digits after the decimal point.
examples.approach: For a fixed x, the weakness is max(maximum subarray sum of (a_i - x), -(minimum subarray sum of (a_i - x))), both computed with a standard O(n) Kadane pass. As a function of x, the weakness is a maximum of two functions, each of which is convex in x (a maximum/minimum subarray sum, viewed as a max/min over a finite set of LINEAR functions of x -- one per subarray -- is itself convex, since a pointwise maximum of linear functions is always convex, and negating a concave minimum keeps it convex too); a maximum of convex functions is convex, so weakness(x) is convex, hence unimodal, and ternary search applies directly on the real line. Run ternary search with a fixed number of iterations (200, far more than needed for 1e-6 precision) over a sufficiently wide range, evaluating weakness(x) via Kadane at each of the two candidate points per iteration, and narrow toward the minimum. Verified by brute-force scanning weakness(x) on a fine grid (step 0.0001) for the sample input, confirming the ternary search converges to the same minimum (x=2, weakness=1.0 for input [1,2,3]).

examples.title: Equalize Pillar Heights at Minimum Total Cost (integer ternary search)
examples.problem:
You are given n pillars, where pillar i currently has height h[i]. You want to choose a single target height T (an integer) and adjust every pillar to have height T, where the cost of adjusting pillar i to height T is |h[i] - T| (moving each unit of height costs 1). Find the target height T that minimizes the total cost, and print T together with the minimum total cost. (If multiple T achieve the same minimum cost, print the smallest such T.)

Input: n, then n integers h[1..n].
Output: two integers: the optimal T, and the minimum total cost.
examples.approach: cost(T) = sum of |h[i] - T| is a sum of convex (absolute-value) functions of T, hence convex, hence unimodal (minimized, with possibly a flat plateau at the median when n is even) -- a textbook target for integer ternary search. Because integer ternary search can behave incorrectly right at the boundary of a very small range or on a plateau, use the robust pattern: shrink the range [lo, hi] only while hi - lo > 2, using two interior points m1, m2 at roughly the 1/3 and 2/3 marks, and comparing cost(m1) <= cost(m2) to decide which side to discard (convexity guarantees the true minimum is never discarded by this rule, even on a plateau, because it never discards past the point where cost stops being provably worse). Once the range has shrunk to at most 3 candidates, brute-force evaluate cost at each remaining integer and take the best (and, for tie-breaking to the smallest T, scan candidates in increasing order and only replace the best on a STRICT improvement). This correctly reproduces the well-known fact that the optimum is the median of h[].

subtopics.name: Custom Comparators & Multi-Key Sorting
subtopics.theory:
Many greedy algorithms are only correct once the input is sorted by exactly the right key -- often a DERIVED key (a ratio, a sum, or a comparison rule between two fields) rather than any single raw field, and sometimes a different sort order for different subsets of the input entirely. Getting this key right is usually justified by an EXCHANGE ARGUMENT: suppose an optimal solution processes two adjacent elements i then j in some order; show that swapping their order never makes the solution worse (and sometimes strictly better) exactly when a certain inequality between their fields holds; that inequality between i's and j's fields is then used to define the comparator, guaranteeing that no adjacent swap can improve on the sorted order, which (by a standard argument extending adjacent transpositions to arbitrary permutations) means the sorted order is optimal among all orderings.

A canonical two-group example: processing 'projects' that each require a minimum resource level to start and then change the resource level by some signed delta. Projects with a non-negative delta (net gainers) should be processed sorted ascending by their requirement -- do the 'cheapest to unlock' ones first to build up resources as fast as possible. Projects with a negative delta (net spenders) should be processed sorted DESCENDING by (requirement + delta), i.e. by their value AFTER completion -- counter-intuitively not by their requirement directly, because what matters for a spender is how much of a safety margin it leaves behind for the remaining spenders, and an exchange argument shows that ordering by post-completion value descending never causes an avoidable failure.

A second common shape: a greedy that needs 'the k best items where quality is judged by a MINIMUM over the selected group, multiplied or combined with a SUM over the group' (e.g. maximize sum(speed) * min(efficiency), or minimize a cost keyed by the max ratio in a hired group). The trick is to sort by the field that appears as a min/max in the objective (efficiency, or wage-to-quality ratio) descending, then scan while maintaining the SUM field (speed, or quality) in a heap of bounded size -- because sorting by the min/max field first guarantees that, at the moment each element is considered, every element seen so far (including the current one) has a min/max-field value at least as large as the current one, so the current element's field value is safely usable as 'the min (or the threshold ratio) of the group so far' without having to re-check every previously chosen element.
subtopics.recognition: A greedy or heap-based approach seems natural, but sorting by the obvious raw field gives wrong answers on small counterexamples; the objective mixes two fields (a per-element requirement/cost and a per-element gain/effect, or a sum together with a min/max), and you suspect the right order is by a DERIVED key (a sum of two fields, a ratio, or 'value after applying the effect') rather than either raw field alone.
subtopics.complexity: O(n log n) for the sort, plus O(n) or O(n log n) for the subsequent greedy/heap scan, so O(n log n) total.

examples.title: Feasibility of Ordering Rating-Changing Projects (two-key exchange-argument sort)
examples.problem:
You start with rating R. You are given n projects; project i requires your CURRENT rating to be at least a[i] to start it, and completing it changes your rating by b[i] (which may be positive or negative). Your rating must never become negative at any point (including immediately after completing a project). Determine whether there exists an order to complete ALL n projects without ever violating these constraints.

Input: n and R, then n pairs a[i] b[i].
Output: "YES" if some valid order exists, otherwise "NO".
examples.approach: Split the projects into two groups: 'gainers' with b[i] >= 0, and 'spenders' with b[i] < 0. Do all gainers first, sorted ascending by a[i] -- an exchange argument shows that if two gainers could be swapped to violate this order and still be feasible, swapping them back to ascending-a order is also feasible (a gainer only helps future rating, so unlocking the cheapest requirement first is never worse). Then do all spenders, sorted DESCENDING by (a[i] + b[i]) -- the rating immediately after completing the project -- again by an exchange argument: for two adjacent spenders i, j, doing i before j requires rating >= max(a[i], a[j] - b[i]) at that point, while doing j before i requires rating >= max(a[j], a[i] - b[j]); algebraic manipulation shows that ordering by descending post-completion value (a[i]+b[i]) never requires a strictly higher minimum starting rating than any other order, so it's always safe to prefer it. Simulate both groups in this fixed order, tracking the running rating and failing immediately if any project's requirement isn't met or if the rating would go negative afterward. This crafted test demonstrates the necessity of the (a+b)-descending rule: sorting spenders by requirement 'a' ascending instead would process a=4 before a=5, whose simulation fails, even though the correct (a+b)-descending order (a=5 before a=4) succeeds from the same starting rating.

examples.title: Course Schedule III (deadline sort + retroactive max-heap swap)
examples.problem:
You are given n courses, course i taking duration[i] days and having a deadline lastDay[i] (you must FINISH it on or before lastDay[i]). You may take the courses in any order, one at a time with no gaps, starting at day 0. Find the maximum number of courses you can take without missing any deadline of a course you commit to finishing.

Input: n, then n pairs duration[i] lastDay[i].
Output: the maximum number of courses that can be taken.
examples.approach: Sort courses ascending by deadline -- this is the key comparator choice, because it lets you consider courses in an order where, once you decide to 'tentatively take' a course, every course considered afterward has an equal or later deadline, so there is never a reason to prefer a not-yet-seen course over one already tentatively scheduled except on duration. Greedily try to take every course in this deadline order, maintaining a running total time and a max-heap of the durations of courses currently scheduled. After tentatively adding a course (adding its duration to the running time and pushing it to the heap), check if the running time now exceeds this course's deadline; if so, the schedule is currently infeasible, so retroactively REMOVE the single longest-duration course scheduled so far (found instantly via the max-heap) -- this is always at least as good as removing the just-added course, since it frees up the most possible time while keeping the same count of courses scheduled, and it cannot violate any earlier deadline (all remaining courses have equal-or-later, already-satisfied deadlines). The final answer is the number of courses remaining in the heap.

subtopics.name: Order Statistics / Quickselect
subtopics.theory:
The k-th order statistic of a collection is simply the k-th smallest (or largest) element. Sorting the whole collection to find it costs O(n log n), but quickselect -- reusing quicksort's partition step without recursing into both sides -- finds it in expected O(n) time. Partition the array around a pivot (ideally chosen randomly to avoid adversarial worst-case inputs) exactly as in quicksort: rearrange so all elements less than the pivot come first, then the pivot itself lands at its final sorted position 'store', then all elements greater than or equal to the pivot follow. If store equals the target index k, the pivot IS the answer; otherwise, recurse into only the half of the array that must contain the k-th element (the left part if k < store, the right part if k > store) -- discarding the other half entirely, which is what turns the expected O(n log n) of full quicksort into an expected O(n) (each recursive call operates on a geometrically shrinking array, summing to O(n) total work in expectation with random pivots).

A second, entirely different family of order-statistics problems asks for the k-th smallest value in an implicitly defined, exponentially large combinatorial set -- e.g. the k-th smallest pairwise distance among all C(n,2) pairs, the k-th smallest pairwise product between two arrays, or the k-th smallest sum choosing one element from each of several sorted lists. Enumerating the whole set is infeasible, but if you can efficiently COUNT how many elements of the set are <= a candidate value v (often via a two-pointer sweep over sorted data, or a per-row binary search), you can binary search on the answer value v itself: search for the smallest v such that count(<=v) >= k. This 'binary search on the answer, count with a cheaper structure' pattern is itself a generalization of order-statistics selection -- instead of partitioning the actual elements (quickselect), you partition the space of POSSIBLE ANSWER VALUES using a monotonic counting function, which is valid whenever count(<=v) is monotonically non-decreasing in v (always true, since a bigger threshold can only include more elements).

Which of the two techniques applies depends on whether you can cheaply materialize or partition the actual elements (use quickselect) versus only cheaply COUNT how many elements satisfy a threshold (use binary-search-on-the-answer with a counting subroutine).
subtopics.recognition: You need the k-th smallest/largest element (or a k-th order statistic of some derived quantity like a difference, product, or sum) without needing the collection fully sorted; if the k-th value comes from an explicit array, quickselect applies; if it comes from an implicitly huge set of combinations, look for a monotonic 'count elements <= v' function and binary search on v.
subtopics.complexity: Expected O(n) time, O(1) extra space for randomized quickselect on an explicit array of n elements; O(n log n) time (sort) plus O(log(range) * (cost of one count)) for binary-search-on-the-answer over an implicit combinatorial set.

examples.title: K-th Smallest Element via Randomized Quickselect
examples.problem:
Given an unsorted array of n distinct integers, find the k-th smallest element (1-indexed: k=1 means the minimum) without fully sorting the array.

Input: n, then n integers, then k.
Output: the k-th smallest element.
examples.approach: Use Hoare-style partitioning with a RANDOMLY chosen pivot (to make worst-case O(n^2) behavior astronomically unlikely regardless of input order): pick a random index in the current subrange, swap that pivot value to the end, then scan the rest of the subrange moving every element smaller than the pivot to the front (tracked by a 'store' index), and finally swap the pivot into position 'store' -- its final sorted position within this subrange. If store equals the 0-indexed target k-1, return the pivot immediately. Otherwise, recurse (via a loop, not actual recursion, to keep it iterative) into only the side of the partition that must contain the target: the left part if the target index is less than store, the right part otherwise. This discards, on average, half the remaining array at each step, giving expected O(n) total work despite each partition step itself costing O(current subrange size). A fixed random seed is used here only so the output is reproducible for testing; a real submission could seed from time or use std::random_device.

examples.title: K-th Smallest Pairwise Distance (binary search on the answer + two pointers)
examples.problem:
Given an array of n integers, consider the multiset of all C(n,2) pairwise absolute differences |nums[i] - nums[j]| for i < j. Find the k-th smallest value in this multiset (1-indexed).

Input: n, then n integers, then k.
Output: the k-th smallest pairwise distance.
examples.approach: Enumerating all C(n,2) distances directly is too slow for large n, but the number of pairs with distance <= v is easy to COUNT for a fixed v: sort the array, then for each right pointer, advance a left pointer forward while nums[right] - nums[left] > v, and add (right - left) to the count (every index from left to right-1 pairs with right to form a distance <= v) -- this two-pointer count runs in O(n) since both pointers only move forward, for a total of O(n) per candidate v. Since count(<=v) is monotonically non-decreasing in v, binary search on v over the range [0, max-min] for the smallest v with count(<=v) >= k; that v is guaranteed to actually be an achievable pairwise distance (not just a threshold), because count(<=v) only changes at values that are themselves actual pairwise distances. Total time is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n log(max-min)) for the binary search with its O(n) counting step.
